title: Rama asks the trees
hook: the hero weeps in the empty forest: God, living as a man, grieves
carry: avatar: god lived a human grief
tomorrow: who has waited years for Rama to walk up her path?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the abduction, and Jatayu, the old bird who fought a king and lost his wings. Nishkama karma: do right, and leave the fruit.

Rama is running. He has chased the golden deer deep into the forest, killed it, and heard it shout in his own voice. Racing back through the trees, he meets Lakshmana coming toward him, alone, and his heart drops. This is the prince who accepted exile in one sentence, who faced fourteen thousand warriors alone, whose face, Valmiki says, didn't change when he lost a kingdom. The brothers reach the clearing together. The hut is there. Sita is not.
screen: `RACING BACK THROUGH THE TREES.` → `THE STEADY ONE.` → `THE HUT IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: What happens next doesn't flatter its hero. Rama runs from tree to tree, calling her name, asking the trees if they've seen her. He asks the deer, and in Valmiki's telling the deer all turn their heads and look south. He weeps until he can barely stand. Then the grief turns into rage. He tells Lakshmana he'll fill the sky with arrows and tear the worlds apart until the gods give her back. It's the younger brother, usually the hothead, who calms him: you're the one who taught everyone patience, he says, in effect. Don't become the storm. Then they find Jatayu, and Rama holds the dying bird. Why would a story about God on earth show him coming apart? On day thirty-six you met avatara: God coming down, born as one of us. Hindus who worship Rama as Vishnu's avatar don't read these tears as a flaw in the story. Many read them as the point. He didn't wear a human life like a costume. He lived it, and a human life includes losing someone you love. Remember the morning his face didn't change at the news of exile. Losing a kingdom, he stayed still. Losing Sita, he can't. And Lakshmana doesn't scold him. He stays beside him, and turns him back toward the search. That's why many devotees bring God their grief without hiding it: the God they pray to has stood in an empty clearing calling a name. When you, or someone strong you love, comes apart, the tradition doesn't say be strong. It says even Rama wept, and someone sat beside him.
screen: `RAMA ASKS THE TREES.` · `LAKSHMANA CALMS THE STORM.` · `AVATAR: GOD LIVES A HUMAN LIFE.` · `GOD ON EARTH, AND HE WEEPS.` · then, large: `EVEN RAMA WEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of a strong person in your life who is grieving, and sit beside them in your mind, the way Lakshmana sits beside Rama. Don't try to fix it. If you pray, say Rama's name softly a few times, the way many Hindus do in hard hours: Ram, Ram. If you don't, just stay with them, unhurried. If a grief of your own comes up, let it sit there too.
Rama breaks. The hero, in the empty forest, asking the trees where she went. The poem doesn't hide it.
Hold onto this: avatar. God lived a human grief, and Lakshmana sat beside him. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 53 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO HAS WAITED YEARS FOR RAMA?`

howItsDone: Rama's lament in the forest is recited and sung in Ramayana readings, and Ramlila performances often stage it as an emotional scene; many devotees speak of Rama's grief as part of the full human life of Vishnu's avatar, and many Hindus say Rama's name in hard hours.

chat.meaning: For Hindus who worship Rama as Vishnu's avatar, his grief is real: God lived a full human life, loss included.

Valmiki.meaning: the poet traditionally credited with the first Ramayana

Jatayu.meaning: the old vulture king who fought Ravana to save Sita

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, who followed him into exile

Sita.meaning: Rama's wife, carried off by Ravana

avatar.meaning: God coming down, born into the world as one of us

Bal Vihar.meaning: a Hindu Sunday school for children, often at the mandir

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Rama's search and lament; Lakshmana calms him, roughly sargas 60–66)
